content: In 2017, a significant meeting took place in Geneva, Switzerland, involving marginalized groups shortly after the release of the WHO 2017 Consolidated Guideline. This event marked a turning point for us. The findings from the guideline strengthened our determination and provided us with evidence-based arguments to advocate for the Ukrainian government to adopt and implement its recommendations. These findings also enabled us to push for the inclusion of women living with HIV in Ukraine's Global Fund funding request, a goal that had previously been unsuccessful due to the perception that we were not a key population of focus. Through the Communities Mobilisation Working Group, we successfully secured funding to address violence experienced by women. This historic investment, the first of its kind, was complemented by the official representation of women living with HIV in the Country Coordinating Mechanism (CCM) since July 2019. In 2018, with the support of the Global Fund, we trained service providers in 10 regions of Ukraine to address the impact of gender-based violence (GBV) on women living with HIV. We also initiated community-led research to monitor GBV among HIV-positive women in prevention, care, and support programs across these regions. The Ukrainian experience is now being used by EWNA to promote similar research at a regional level. With support from UNFPA, we conducted a values and preferences survey in Moldova. On the International Day of Action for Women’s Health, we launched a community-friendly Russian translation of the WHO Consolidated Guideline on sexual and reproductive health and rights (SRHR) for women living with HIV. On June 4, 2019, after two years of advocacy, an order from the Ministry of Health came into effect, allowing women living with HIV with undetectable viral loads to access IVF services. The WHO SRHR Guideline and the Global Values and Preferences Survey (GVPS) have been instrumental in helping us understand the scope of our rights. These tools have empowered us to advocate for better quality of life and reduced stigma, particularly self-stigma, for women living with HIV. For example, L’Orangelis Thomas Negrón, an HIV-positive activist from Puerto Rico, has been a key figure in this movement. She has worked tirelessly to ensure that women, especially young women living with HIV, can live free of stigma and enjoy fulfilling lives. Her work includes co-founding Pangea, a positive youth group, and collaborating with feminist and LGBTQIA+ groups on SRHR issues, including safe abortion access and post-abortion care. L’Orangelis has also been involved in workshops that focus on body autonomy, sexuality, and empowerment for women living with HIV. These workshops include guided meditations, art therapy, and discussions about sexual health and pleasure. They provide a safe space for women to explore their feelings, share their experiences, and build supportive communities. In some workshops, participants use 3D models of female anatomy to learn about their bodies and even conduct self-examinations, which is a powerful act of reclaiming autonomy. The workshops also address topics like gender-based violence and mental well-being. L’Orangelis has conducted these workshops in various countries, including Argentina, Peru, Mexico, South Africa, and Zimbabwe, adapting them to the cultural contexts of each region. For instance, discussions about sexuality are more open in Latin America, where many young women identify as feminists, compared to Southern Africa, where traditional patriarchal cultures and stigma make such conversations more challenging. In Puerto Rico, L’Orangelis has focused on working with young women and creating youth groups to build networks of support. She plans to develop a manual to help other women conduct similar workshops across the country, emphasizing the importance of solidarity and community-building before advocating for national SRHR policies. She is also adapting workshops for transgender, queer, and non-binary individuals, recognizing their unique needs and perspectives. The GVPS and the WHO Guideline have been transformative tools, enabling women living with HIV to understand their rights and translate them into practical actions. These efforts are not just about policy but about creating spaces where women can connect, share, and empower each other to lead fulfilling lives free from stigma and fear.
